en_segments: Therefore , even if there are witnesses, etc. The Shach asks from the ruling below in siman 400 concerning two oxen that gored, where the injured party says that the larger ox caused the damage and the owner says that the smaller ox caused it. The Gemara at the end of chapter HaManiach compares this to one who claimed wheat and the other admitted barley, where he is exempt. Yet the Mechaber rules, following Rambam, that if there are witnesses to the goring, the injured party collects from the smaller ox. The Shach seeks to distinguish between the cases. What is stated here, that even if there are witnesses he is exempt, means that they testify clearly concerning barley. Below, however, the witnesses saw a goring but did not know which ox gored. So too here, if they know that there was a loan but do not know whether it was wheat or barley, the claimant should at least recover the value of the barley, because he can say: whichever way you look at it, if the witnesses are telling the truth, give me at least the barley. These are his words. This is difficult, however, for if so, why did the Mechaber omit the rule that where witnesses testify merely that there was a loan, the claimant at least recovers the barley? More fundamentally, I do not understand the reasoning. What sort of whichever way you look at it argument is there? If the witnesses testified to wheat, give him wheat, and if they testified to barley, give him barley. But where they testify explicitly to barley, the claimant has no right to the barley. What difference is there whether they speak doubtfully or decisively? In the end, if the truth is that the debt was barley, then by claiming wheat he admitted and waived the barley. How can money be extracted because of a doubt? This is particularly difficult in light of what appears from the Gemara there, and as I will write below in explaining Rambam, that where the tortfeasor says he is uncertain and the injured party makes a definite claim, it is treated as one who claimed wheat, etc. What difference is there between an admission by his own mouth and testimony of witnesses? An admission by a litigant is stronger than one hundred witnesses. I therefore do not fully understand the basis for this distinction. There is also a precision to be noted in Rambam himself. Not only did he fail to mention in Hilchot To'en VeNitan, in the discussion of one who claims wheat and the other admits barley, the rule that where witnesses exist he pays the lesser amount, but even in Hilchot Nizkei Mamon he inserted this rule in the middle of the paragraph dealing with two pursuing oxen, one large and one small, saying that if there are witnesses, etc. He did not place it at the end after all the cases taught in the Mishnah, namely one tam and one mu'ad, and two oxen pursuing two others. For it is as though he waived it, etc. Know that the Rosh, at the end of chapter HaManiach, writes that Rashi and Tosafot explain that the reason the claimant is exempt from the barley is that he is treated as though he waived the barley. The Rosh writes: I am astonished at this reasoning, because it is common for a person to have several claims against another and not wish to demand all of them at once. He may demand only one of them and nevertheless has not waived the others. Furthermore, this is not comparable to our Mishnah. In the Mishnah there is an admission, for by claiming that the larger ox caused the damage he admitted that the smaller ox did not cause it. This is not a waiver. Therefore, even if we say that in the Mishnah the defendant is liable because the claimant's statement is not treated as an admission, since he intended only to enhance his recovery by claiming the larger ox, it can still be that one who claims wheat is exempt from the barley because his failure to claim the barley constitutes waiver. Conversely, even if we say that in the Mishnah the defendant is exempt because the claimant's statement is an admission, it can still be that in the case of wheat and barley the defendant remains liable for the barley because we do not say that the claimant waived it. I therefore explain the case of claiming wheat as comparable to the Mishnah only where the claimant says, "I lent you wheat on that day and at that hour," and the other responds, "It was barley." If he had lent him both commodities at that same time, he would have claimed both, since they arose simultaneously. His failure to claim the barley therefore constitutes an admission that the defendant does not owe him barley. These are the Rosh's words. Many explanations have been offered regarding the Rosh's intent and the difference between admission and waiver. Rabbenu Yerucham, his student, writes in Netiv 3, part 2, that according to the Rosh, if the defendant stands by his words and affirms them, saying, "You have barley in my possession," he is liable for the barley. His words require study. The Shach explains Rabbenu Yerucham to mean that beit din does not compel the defendant to pay, because the defendant can say that the claimant already admitted that he owes him nothing, but if the defendant himself fails to pay he is considered a robber. This is incomprehensible. Whichever way one looks at it, if we say that the claimant's statement is not an admission that effects waiver, why should beit din not compel payment? The defendant has admitted owing barley. How can he escape by saying, "The claimant admitted that I owe him nothing," when we know that his present contention is false and foolish? We know that he now states in beit din, just as he stated before, that he owes barley. But even according to the version of the Gemara in which Rav Pappa asks whether the Mishnah refutes Rabbah bar Natan, and Rav Pappa holds that half damages are compensatory, the matter can still be explained. Quite apart from our issue, one must understand the Gemara's establishment of the middle clause as a case where the injured party says he is uncertain and the tortfeasor makes a definite claim. Tosafot ask why this clause is not also needed to reject Sumchus. They answer that since there is partial admission, Sumchus would say that the parties divide. Tosafot later write, s.v. ra'ui litol, that the clauses are both necessary. The first clause teaches that even where the injured party makes a definite claim and the tortfeasor is uncertain, the Sages still apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. The case of the larger and smaller ox teaches that where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, Sumchus nevertheless requires division. At first glance this is difficult from the Mishnah in Bava Metzia 97, where the renter says that the rented animal died and the owner says that he does not know, and the renter is exempt. The Gemara establishes that Mishnah, according to Rav Nachman, as a case of partial admission: the owner claimed three cows and the renter admitted one. Accordingly, in the first clause he is one who cannot swear and must pay. If so, according to Sumchus, why should it matter that the owner says he is uncertain? Since there is partial admission, Sumchus should require division rather than a complete exemption. Yet the Gemara there establishes the Mishnah according to Sumchus. Similarly, in Bava Metzia 100, where the Mishnah discusses one who exchanged property and where there were two slaves, the seller says, "I sold the smaller one," and the buyer says, "I do not know," the smaller slave is awarded to the buyer. That case too involves partial admission, as the Gemara establishes in explaining the clause requiring an oath, namely that the dispute concerns the value of the smaller slave, etc. If so, Sumchus should require division there as well, yet that Mishnah too is according to Sumchus. Rav Nachman rejects that principle only where the definite claimant seeks to extract money from the possessor, because the possessor's monetary chazakah is powerful. But where the possessor himself makes the definite claim, even Rav Nachman agrees that the definite claim is superior, since the possessor's chazakah supports it. And at a particular time, etc. This is the view of the Rosh. Maharshal, in Yam Shel Shlomo, writes that the formulation is stated without qualification and therefore implies that the rule applies even if the two loans did not occur on the same day. Addressing the Rosh's difficulty, he explains that after the defendant admitted the barley, the claimant returned to demanding wheat and did not mention barley in his renewed claim. This demonstrates that he waived the barley. The Shach writes that even the Rosh agrees with this rule where the circumstances are as Maharshal describes, namely that the claimant returned and again demanded wheat. Even if the two loans did not arise together, he is then exempt from the barley. The Rosh merely found it strained to interpret Rabbah bar Natan's statement in this manner, especially since the Rosh raised another difficulty against Rashi's explanation based on waiver. See there. In my opinion, Tosafot provide proof for Maharshal's view. Moreover, even the Rosh, who explains the rule in terms of admission, means that the admission occurs only when the claimant returns and again demands the wheat, not beforehand. Nevertheless, the Rosh still does not accept that this is a waiver where the two loans did not arise together, because the fact that the claimant returned to demand wheat proves nothing about the separate barley debt. Since the two debts did not arise together, he had no reason to concern himself with demanding the other one at that time. My difficulty is with Tosafot, s.v. leima, who ask why the Mishnah could not follow Rabban Gamliel, who holds that where one claims wheat and the defendant admits barley, the defendant is liable. Tosafot answer that even Rabban Gamliel agrees that the defendant is exempt from paying the barley itself. Rabban Gamliel holds only that the admission nevertheless creates an oath of partial admission. See there. I do not understand this. Suppose a claimant says to another, "You owe me one hundred gold coins. Fifty are waived to you, and pay me the other fifty," and the defendant responds, "I never owed you except fifty, and those fifty are waived by you." Could one imagine that the defendant is liable for an oath of partial admission? He has admitted owing nothing that remains payable. There could be no clearer case of total denial. It therefore appears that Tosafot agree with Maharshal. On the claimant's first demand there is not yet any waiver, because a person does not necessarily demand all his claims at once. Only after the defendant admits barley and the claimant then returns to demand wheat does the principal waiver occur. Accordingly, at the moment when the defendant admitted the barley, his statement was still a complete and effective monetary admission. And one should not infer against the Rosh that, in any event, this oath itself is difficult. The claimant has seized the barley, so the amount admitted is already in his hands and would seem to be heilech, since the very money corresponding to the defendant's admission is already possessed by the claimant. One may answer that according to the reasoning the Rosh was discussing, seizure works because of a whichever way you look at it argument: either give me the barley, or I will retain what I seized toward the value of the wheat. On that theory, even seizure after the parties have already appeared in judgment is effective. It therefore is not heilech, because at the time of the defendant's admission the admitted amount was not yet in the claimant's hands. This is straightforward. Nor should one argue that the Rosh could have proven his position more simply. If claiming wheat and admitting barley referred to a barley loan made at another time, and the claimant's failure to demand that barley loan constituted waiver, then the same should be true even where he claimed wheat lent in Nisan and the defendant admitted wheat lent in Tishrei. The defendant should be exempt because the claimant did not demand the Tishrei loan and therefore evidently waived it. One may answer that the Rosh writes in the sugya of the borrowed and rented animals that people do not confuse wheat with barley. By contrast, they may confuse times. The claimant may confuse Tishrei with Nisan. Accordingly, where both claims concern wheat, the defendant can say that the loan he admits is the very loan being claimed, except that the claimant erred regarding the date. This resolves the point. Still, according to what I wrote, one could say that even when the barley itself is exempt, an oath may remain because the defendant made a partial admission, while the Sages exempt him from the oath only because they hold that the admission must be of the same kind as the claim. If so, where both claims concern wheat, the admission is certainly of the same kind as the claim and the defendant would not be exempt from an oath. Rabbah bar Natan, however, states a complete exemption. Yet this is not a sufficient answer either, because if the defendant admitted the same quantity of wheat that the claimant demanded, there is no denied amount at all. What partial admission would there be upon which to impose an oath?

And if he seized it. This is the view of the Rif and Rambam. The Rosh, however, asks according to his approach that if so, the Gemara should also have established the middle clause as a case of seizure rather than as one where the injured party says he is uncertain and the tortfeasor says he is certain. The Shach writes to resolve this. Before considering his resolution, however, we must understand the Rosh's question itself. Why does the Rosh not ask the same question against his own approach? Let both clauses be established as cases where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain. One must answer, as Rashi and Tosafot do, that if so the two clauses would be redundant. But if the Rif's explanation is that both clauses concern seizure, the same redundancy exists. It is true that the Rosh was careful on this point and wrote that the middle clause should have been established as a case of seizure and the final clause as a case of a definite claim against an uncertain one. Yet the need for this is unclear. What do we gain? The difficulty against Rabbah bar Mamal that the Mishnah does not deal with two definite claims remains. Surely the first, middle, and final clauses are all meant to parallel one another. As the Gemara itself explains, the final clause involves the injured party making a definite claim, the tortfeasor being uncertain, and seizure, while the middle clause has the reverse, the tortfeasor certain and the injured party uncertain, and the first clause again has the tortfeasor uncertain and the injured party certain. All the clauses thus contain some combination of definite and uncertain claims. If we reverse the explanations, the clauses are still parallel. The final clause would have the injured party uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, while the middle and first clauses would have the injured party certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, with the middle clause involving seizure. What, then, has been gained? The original difficulty remains. The Maadanei Melech apparently seeks to resolve this by saying that the way of the Gemara is to give the more comfortable explanation first and only afterward resort to a strained one. Thus, on the first difficulty the Gemara should have answered with seizure. This is not sufficient, especially as a basis for rejecting the Rif. Who can weigh the Gemara's answers so precisely as to say that the explanation involving uncertainty by the injured party is more comfortable than the explanation involving seizure? Seizure is itself entirely unmentioned in the Mishnah. It therefore appears that the Rosh follows the view of the Nimukei Yosef regarding the case where the claimant says that the larger mu'ad ox caused the damage and the other says that the smaller mu'ad ox caused it. And there is a clear proof for the Rif that the seizure explanation applies to the first clause as well. We must explain Rav Pappa's establishment of the middle clause as one where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, and the first clause in the reverse, with the injured party certain and the tortfeasor uncertain. Although the Mishnah says "No, rather," which ordinarily indicates two definite claims, Tosafot and Maharsha explain that the clause includes such a case but that Sumchus's disagreement is relevant only to the case of uncertainty. At first glance, why was Rav Pappa forced to make the first and middle clauses only imperfectly parallel, with uncertainty on opposite sides? It would seem simpler to establish both as cases where both parties are uncertain. In such a case Sumchus and the Sages disagree directly. It is true that the middle clause also includes the case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, which explains the words "No, rather," but there would then be no novelty in saying that Sumchus does not require division in that subcase. One could hardly say that the entire first clause is superfluous, because if it comes merely to teach that Sumchus requires division where both are uncertain, many Mishnayot already establish that rule, such as the beginning of chapter HaParah and the Mishnayot concerning the borrowed and rented animals and concerning an exchange. Nor is it necessary to teach that the Sages disagree even there. The value of the barley. The Sema writes that the reason is that since the claimant is already in possession, he can say, "I neither admitted nor waived the barley. I merely did not wish to demand everything at once." These are his words. At first glance they are incomprehensible. According to the Rama, seizure helps specifically if it occurred before the admission, but not afterward. If the Sema's reasoning were correct, seizure afterward should also help, because the claimant could say, "I know that I did not waive it." One cannot answer that this would be seizure after the doubt arose, because where the possessor makes a definite claim, seizure is effective even after the doubt arose, as the Rosh writes in Ketubot and Bava Metzia. See what I wrote above in the rules of seizure. This is particularly so according to the Mechaber, who holds that seizure even after the doubt arises is effective. We must therefore say that the Sema's reason was written only according to the opinion that seizure is effective even afterward, not according to those who distinguish based on the timing of seizure. Yet the Sema himself, in seif katan 26, cites the Nimukei Yosef's view distinguishing between seizure before the claimant's retraction and seizure afterward. His words therefore remain difficult. The Tur explicitly gives a different reason. He writes: since the claimant seized the barley, his failure to demand it is not considered an admission, because he can say, "I did not demand the barley because I was already in possession of it." This is a different explanation from the Sema's. Still, even the Rosh requires explanation. According to his own view, seizure helps only in the case of the two oxen. He writes: therefore, if the injured party seized before coming to beit din, even in the presence of witnesses, he collects according to what the tortfeasor says. Why does the Rosh require seizure specifically before coming to beit din? In the case of the two injured animals, the explanation that "I did not demand the smaller one because I was already in possession of it" seems inapplicable. The injured party cannot truthfully mean to demand both the large and the small ox, because the two claims are mutually exclusive. If the larger ox caused the damage, the smaller did not. Once he asserts in beit din that the larger ox caused the damage, he can no longer say that the smaller ox did. One might answer that this reason is needed only where the claimant could have claims regarding both items, whereas where the claims are mutually exclusive no such reason is necessary. But if so, the Rosh's objection to the Rif would fail. With wheat and barley it is possible that both claims are true, whereas with one large and one small ox both claims cannot be true.
